title: I made a pixel-art mud-racing game in 3 days by directing an AI coding agent. Here's the workflow.
author: LCRGaming
selftext:
Sludgehammer is a chunky, pixelated 3D mud racer: 13 tracks, a demolition derby, trucks that lose wheels, catch fire and explode, and a twister that comes down mid-race. It's built in Godot 4. I didn't write the code. I directed Claude Code (Anthropic's coding agent) and played every build. Some numbers: 3 days, 100+ commits, about 15,000 lines of GDScript and shaders.



Play it free (Windows, macOS, Linux): [https://badr3qu3st.itch.io/sludgehammer](https://badr3qu3st.itch.io/sludgehammer)

Gameplay reel: [https://youtu.be/u9XbJ4V68XA](https://youtu.be/u9XbJ4V68XA)



\*\*What worked:\*\*

1. \*\*A design doc first.\*\* The game, its scope and its milestones lived in one doc: art test, driving, crashes, the pack, the cup. Each milestone wasn't done until I'd played it and said so.

2. \*\*Everything built in code.\*\* No models and no sound files. The trucks, tracks and crowds are boxes put together in code, and every sound is made in code from noise and tones. The only outside assets are the music, made in Suno from prompts the agent wrote. That kept everything as text the agent could read, change and diff.

3. \*\*It checks its work by looking, not by guessing.\*\* The game takes test switches: a bot drives, \`--shot\` saves a picture, \`--secs\` lists every sound heard, \`--perf\` prints the frame rate, and there are fixed cameras for close-ups. So the agent takes a screenshot or records a clip and looks at it before saying something works. For the audio pass it measured every sound's loudness with ffmpeg. That's how it found the smallest crash sound playing louder than a big one.

4. \*\*I give feedback in plain words.\*\* "The tornado should be pointier as it comes down and spread when it hits the ground." "The card when you hit someone is too big." It goes looking for references when it needs them, changes the game, takes new pictures and shows me. The tornado took about 15 rounds. That's fine.

5. \*\*A notes file that remembers what broke.\*\* The repo has a notes file the agent reads first: how each system works, every bug, and why the code looks the way it does. New sessions don't relearn old lessons.

6. \*\*Commit and push after every change.\*\* Small steps, and any bad change is easy to undo.



\*\*What bit us:\*\*

\- A build that didn't compile opened a black, frozen window on my screen. The rule now: check it compiles headless before opening anything.

\- Some looks need a human eye. "Make it funnier" and "that reads as a big blank card" were my calls; the agent's job was finding the cause and fixing it.



The release trailer was cut the same way: the agent recorded real races, found the beats in the song, and cut every shot on a phrase with ffmpeg. The release went the same way too: it exported the three builds, signed and notarized the Mac one, built the itch page and pushed the builds with butler, while I checked each step.



Happy to answer questions about the setup.

comments.author: Bananaskovitch
comments.body:
The "in X days" are not as impressive as people think. We get it, it's possible to produce a tech demo in a number of days. But trying to makreting that and telling everyone about it is a bit cringe, ngl. These are not much than model benchmarks. 

Even with AI, good games take a long time to make. Nobody except kids and people that hasn't catch up yet on AI capabilities on gamedev are impressed.

replies.author: LCRGaming
replies.body: I'm not trying to impress you or anyone else. Just stating facts. I've been making games since the 90s. It was a fun project, that's all. Sorry you have to hate. If I decide I like it, I'll go back and polish it. It's free and was fun to do. My last game took me six months, the one before that over a year. So what?

replies.author: Bananaskovitch
replies.body: Sorry to have unleashed on you. I am growing tired of this clickbait pattern "I made this game in X days/hours" that is flooding on YouTube and social media and I snapped. I wish you the best with your projects.

replies.author: LCRGaming
replies.body: No worries. I just really have fun making stuff. I've never made a racing game because I suck at them horribly. No clickbait here, just generally interested if anyone likes it so I can make it better. I built games in Flash and Director for years and no one cared. I figured it's kinda the same now, but sometimes you get that one person that really loves it and has a great time. That's what I'm about. It'll stay free unless someone wants to buy me a beer so I left donation as optional. It's all about fun for me and sharing new stuff that pops in my head. Cheers!

comments.author: IndiBestEngineer
comments.body: similar setup here but browser games, plain typescript and canvas, phaser on a couple. the part that saved me the most was a separate qa agent that only plays the build in a browser (window sizes, touch, save, a few minutes of play) and drops screenshots, plus a release agent that says go / no-go before i submit anywhere. neither can edit code, so they can't quietly "fix" what they're supposed to report. did you play every build yourself the whole 3 days?

replies.author: LCRGaming
replies.body: Absolutely played every build. Still playing it and finding things to fix or add. Thinking about trying a split screen local play next after I run some performance tests and improve some of the models.

replies.author: IndiBestEngineer
replies.body: split screen local would be great for a racer. good luck with the perf tests.
